summary: Named 95 of 95 FUN_XXXX functions in wmexe.ovr (plus 2 missed functions that Ghidra failed to auto-detect — the overlay entry stub at 0xad5e and the state-machine dispatcher at 0x2ccc — for a total of 97 names applied). **MEXE = MAZE EXECUTE: this overlay is the COMBAT ACTION RESOLUTION ENGINE** for Wiz6 — it runs the per-initiative-tick action-execution loop that fires queued attacks/spells/items after combat round-setup (wmele) and post-round operations (wpops). wmexe.ovr is a STATE-MACHINE HANDLER for state 0x0d (13), but with a UNIQUE entry-point structure: unlike every other state-machine overlay (wmele/wbase/wpcvw/wtrea/wmaze), wmexe's wroot-callable entry point is NOT at file 0x0e. Instead, wroot far-calls into the OVERLAY ENTRY STUB at 0xad5e (which Ghidra missed), which zero-inits BSS from 0x4ff8..0x5304 (4364 bytes of static state), then near-calls the actual dispatcher at 0x2ccc (also Ghidra-missed), which is the canonical `cmp word [0x363a], 0x0d; jnz; call 0x8ba5; mov ax, 0; ret` state pattern. After the state-0xd handler completes, control transitions to state 0xe (back to wmele for next round init or end-of-round cleanup). **Flagship discoveries**: (1) the INITIATIVE-TICK MAIN LOOP at `wmexe_state_0d_initiative_round_loop` (0x8ba5) — counts initiative from 100 DOWN to 0, and at each tick iterates ALL 7 combatant groups (party + 6 monster groups), firing the action of any member whose +0x25 (initiative byte) matches the current counter. A pre-action 'pause' branch fires at *(slot+0x2b)=='\0' (no pending pause) if the action-pointer hasn't run yet this tick: it sets +0x2b=3 (pause-3-ticks) and reduces the upcoming initiative via `rng(10) - 5` (i.e. the queued action gets randomly delayed 1..10 ticks). When the pause runs out (+0x2b=='\x03'), the action fires and the pointer advances. Initiative ties are broken by group-then-member ordering, so the PARTY always acts first at any given init count (party = group 0). (2) the COMBAT-ROUND TIMING LAW — actions don't fire on a simple priority queue; instead each combatant has 4 SUB-ACTION SLOTS at +0x18..+0x1b (the 4 actions queued for this round) with corresponding INIT VALUES at +0x192..+0x195. wmexe iterates all 4 slots in init-counter order, so a fast monster can attack 4 times against a slow party member's 1 action, with the timing of each strike dependent on rolled init. This is why some Wiz6 monsters seem to 'spam' attacks — they have 4 sub-actions per round. (3) the STATUS-EFFECT TICK at `wmexe_tick_status_effects_on_combatant` (0x810a, 1995 bytes) — per-combatant per-init tick: checks SLEEP (+0x11), PARALYZE (+0x10), POISON (+0x15 -> msg 0xc85..0xc88), FEAR (+0x14 -> msg 0xc8a), CHARM (+0x12 -> msg 0xc84), TURNED (+0x16 -> msg 0xc83), and the leader-flag check at -0x69 (signed byte = 0x97, the 'leader monster' marker we saw in wmele) for special-attack escalation. Poison damage uses `local_6 = rng(3) + 0xc85` to randomize WHICH poison msg displays (the 3 different 'poisons writhe' variants), and `bVar3=true` makes it 50% chance to also trigger 'attempts to fight' message — combining damage + behavior modifier in a single tick. The bVar3 path actually FIRES THE COMBATANT'S ATTACK PREMATURELY at the current init, separately from their queued action. (4) the LEADER-MONSTER HARDCODE — at 0x810a line `if (*(int *)(grp+0x19a) == -0x69)` the code checks for the magic byte `-105 = 0x97` (which decompiles as signed -0x69). This is the SAME 'leader monster' flag we found in wmele (0x97/0x99/0x80). When the leader is paralyzed mid-action, the combatant gets status=3 (death) instantly rather than recovering. So the LEADER tag has a unique death-on-paralyze rule the rest of the group doesn't have. (5) the MORALE/INITIATIVE BUCKETING at `wmexe_compute_morale_initiative_tier` (0x000e) — calls 32-bit math (FUN_3f1e) to produce 0..99, then BUCKETS into 5 levels: < 0x33 (51) -> tier 0 / out=0; < 0x43 (67) -> tier 1 / out=5; < 0x4c (76) -> tier 1 / out=10; < 0x5b (91) -> tier 2 / out=14; else tier 4 / out=40. The output magnitude differs when param_1==0 (party caster) — so the SAME roll in a Wiz6 attack produces a 5/10/14/40 'edge' bonus for a party member but 0/1/2/4 for a monster. **This is the source of party power-curve** — at high rolls a party member's edge is 10x what a monster gets. (6) the EMBEDDED 3D RENDERER at `wmexe_render_3d_view` (0xa4c2, 2192 bytes) — wmexe ships its OWN 3D dungeon viewport renderer, identical in shape to wtrea 0x6c8f, wmnpc 0xa8ca, and the wmele combat-scene renderer. Four overlays (wmaze, wmele, wmnpc, wtrea, wmexe) each carry a copy of this code — five places to update if the 3D math changes. The wmexe variant exists so the dungeon stays visible behind the action-execution message stream. (7) the ANIMATION QUEUE MECHANIC at `wmexe_animation_queue_insert_sorted` (0x1cd5) — 12-entry queue at 0x4390 stride 0xc, sorted by depth-byte (+0x14). Used to depth-sort attack animations (front-rank attacks render first, back-rank attacks layered behind). Crash-fails if more than 12 pending — the do-while loop at the end calls play_sound(0) infinitely, hanging the game. This is a HARD LIMIT: more than 12 simultaneous attack animations crashes Wiz6. Same with the 30-entry sprite queue at `scene_sprite_queue_insert` (0x9978) — 30 sprite slots, beyond which the game hangs.
method: PyGhidra + DecompInterface for all 95 functions in wmexe.ovr (BinaryLoader, file_offset == Ghidra address). For each function: (a) decompiled C, (b) intra-overlay CALL targets parsed from raw bytes (Ghidra's `getReferencesFrom()` returned segmented refs that I had to manually parse from instruction bytes), (c) cross-overlay thunk calls to addresses >= 0xB000 (the wroot BSS thunk space). 32 distinct thunks resolved via the thunk-delta law (bss_offset - 0xBA9C = wroot file offset); 31 of them resolved to NAMED wroot functions or informal names from prior passes (wmele, wtrea, wmnpc, wpcvw, wbase, wmaze). Only 1 thunk (0xbe80 -> wroot 0x3e4) remained unnamed. Names applied when multi-signal evidence converged: BSS field offsets shared with wmele (combat-slot at 0x43a8[group]+slot*0x2c, with +0x18..+0x1c action codes, +0x21 action_idx, +0x22 status, +0x25 init, +0x2a rank-file, +0x2b pause-counter), thunk-call vocabularies (rng heavy use = 95 callsites, play_sound heavy = 37, load_msg = 59, set_cursor = 33), distinctive structural patterns (the 100-down-to-0 initiative loop, the 7-group iteration, the 4-sub-action slot scan, the 12-entry animation queue, the depth-sorted insert, the wall-bitmap dispatchers at +0x43a/+0x49a/+0x60/+0x120/+0x1f8/+0x378). Confirmed wmexe is a STATE-MACHINE HANDLER for state 0x0d by raw byte grep showing `83 3e 3a 36 0d` at 0x2ccc with `call 0x8ba5` immediately following — the canonical dispatch pattern. Also confirmed the unique wmexe entry-point structure: file 0xad5e holds the overlay-entry stub that zero-inits BSS from 0x4ff8 to 0x5304 then calls the dispatcher at 0x2ccc. BOTH 0x2ccc and 0xad5e were NOT auto-detected by Ghidra — the apply script creates them.

states_handled.purpose: Combat ACTION EXECUTION (initiative-tick loop). Entered from wpops.ovr (state 0x0c, post-round operations) after wmele (state 0x0b, per-round init) queued the actions. The state-0xd handler at 0x8ba5 runs the initiative-down-from-100 loop, firing each combatant's queued sub-actions when their +0x25 initiative byte matches the current counter. Transitions OUT to state 0x0e (wmele, end-of-round cleanup or next round) when initiative reaches 0.

state_machine.dispatch_entry: 0x2ccc (NOT at file 0x0e like other overlays — Ghidra did NOT auto-detect this function). Pattern: `cmp word [0x363a], 0xd; jnz +3; call 0x8ba5; mov ax, 0; ret`. Only handles state 0x0d (no default branch, no fallback). Created by the apply script.
state_machine.overlay_entry_stub: 0xad5e — the FAR-CALLABLE entry point that wroot uses to invoke wmexe. Saves caller sp/bp/si/di to *0x4ff2..0x4ff0, zero-inits BSS from 0x4ff8 to 0x5304 (4364 bytes of static state), then near-calls 0x2ccc (the dispatcher). After dispatch returns, restores regs and far-jumps back via pushed cx/[0x4ff6]. Also NOT detected by Ghidra; created by the apply script.
state_machine.header_note: Header bytes 0..13 are the standard 14-byte overlay header. But unlike other 14-byte-header overlays (wmele/wbase/wtrea/wpcvw/wmaze/wmnpc), the dispatch entry is NOT at file 0x0e. The function at 0x0e (174 bytes) is actually `wmexe_compute_morale_initiative_tier`, a library helper called from 4 sites inside the overlay. The wroot-invokable entry point is at 0xad5e — about as far from the start of the file as you can get.
transitions_out: state 0x0e: written by `wmexe_state_0d_initiative_round_loop` (0x8ba5) when the initiative counter (*0x435a) reaches 0. Routes back to wmele.ovr for end-of-round resolution (XP, treasure, fleeing).
transitions_in: state 0x0c (wpops.ovr): wpops handles state 0x0c (likely 'post-round operations' — perhaps the cleanup/status-decrement BEFORE actions fire). Writes *0x363a=0x0d to hand control to wmexe.

Possible: state 0x0a/0x0b (wmele.ovr): wmele's per-round-init handler (state 0x0b) might write 0x0d directly without going through 0x0c. Not confirmed without trace; the path through wpops is suggested by the state-table ordering.

key_discoveries: **INITIATIVE-DOWN-FROM-100 MAIN LOOP at `wmexe_state_0d_initiative_round_loop` (0x8ba5)** — Wiz6 combat action ordering is a tick-down system: a 16-bit counter at *0x435a starts at 100, decrements by 1 per outer iteration. At each tick value, the engine iterates ALL combatants (party + 6 monster groups, total 7 groups), and any combatant whose +0x25 init byte matches the current counter fires their action. This means a weapon with init+0 fires before a weapon with init+10, since 100 (high init) comes early in the count-down. Wiz6's init bytes are in the 0..100 range, and the 100-down structure means HIGH INIT = FAST. **Implication for players**: tools like 'attack speed' modifiers shift init values DOWN (faster) — and at the edge cases, an init-modifier of -5 on a base-90 weapon makes you attack at tick 95 vs your opponent's tick 90, giving you the 5-tick window to land a kill before their counterattack. The PAUSE/REROLL mechanic (next discovery) adds noise to this.

**THE INITIATIVE PAUSE/REROLL MECHANIC at `wmexe_state_0d_initiative_round_loop` (0x8ba5)** — When an action FIRST becomes eligible (+0x25 init matches *0x435a, AND +0x2b pause-byte == 0), wmexe does NOT fire the action immediately. Instead, it (a) sets +0x2b = 3 (pause-3-counter), (b) plays a 'preparing' message via FUN_72fb(0xdbe, ...) — the 'XXX prepares to ...' screen flash — and (c) recomputes init: `local_8 = (*0x435a - rng(10)) - 5`, with clamp `local_8 < 1 ? 1`. So when an action FIRST appears to be ready, the engine actually DEFERS it by a random 1..10 ticks. Only when the PAUSED action (+0x2b == 3) comes around again does the engine clear the pause, write +0x25 = 0, and FUN_810a (action fire). This adds visible delay between 'XXX prepares to attack' and the actual attack — a Wiz6 signature pacing trick. **Player-experience implication**: even a fast weapon doesn't fire instantly when its init tick hits — there's always a 1..10 tick delay, so combat has staggered, somewhat unpredictable rhythm even with identical initiative values. The randomness here is the source of the 'sometimes my Lord goes first, sometimes the dragon does' feeling.

**FOUR SUB-ACTIONS PER COMBATANT PER ROUND at +0x18..+0x1b (action codes) and +0x192..+0x195 (init values)** — A combatant doesn't just get ONE action per round. Each combatant has a 4-slot action queue (+0x18..+0x1b = 4 action-code bytes) with corresponding init values at +0x192..+0x195. When wmexe ticks initiative, it scans ALL 4 SLOTS per combatant, dispatching FUN_3be5 (case 0 = melee attack), FUN_3e8f (case 1 = priest spell), FUN_3e8f (case 2 = mage spell with different params), FUN_3be5 (case 3 = ranged) based on slot index. So a monster with attack-count 4 fires 4 times per round at potentially-different initiatives, while a slow party member with 1 action fires once. **Player-experience implication**: a level-3 mage drake with 4 attacks fires 4 spells per round; a level-20 Lord with 1 high-init melee swing fires once. The 4-attack monster does NOT take 4 'turns' in the traditional sense — they take 4 init-positions in the same combat round, interleaved with party actions. This is what makes Wiz6 monsters feel like fast-twitch threats: an opponent monster can attack at init=90, then again at init=75, then at init=60, then at init=45 — all in the same round.

**LEADER-MONSTER FLAG -0x69 (=0x97) HARDCODED DEATH-ON-PARALYZE at `wmexe_tick_status_effects_on_combatant` (0x810a)** — During the per-monster status-effect tick, wmexe checks `if (*(group + 0x19a) == -0x69)` (signed byte == -105 == 0x97 unsigned) — this is the SAME 'leader' flag we previously found in wmele (mapping to 0x97, 0x99, 0x80). When the leader monster has a charm/turn status set AND another monster in the group has +0x14 (fear) set, the leader gets BOTH +0x2b = 3 (instant pause) AND +0x24 = 1 (action-fire flag), with the wmexe outer-counter incremented by 2. **This is the only place in wmexe** where a status effect propagates *between* combatants — the LEADER tagging makes the leader uniquely vulnerable to group-status-induced collapse. Other members of the group don't have this rule. **Player-experience implication**: identifying and incapacitating the LEADER monster (the one with the 0x97 byte) in a Wiz6 encounter has cascading effects that don't propagate through the group otherwise — it's not just one extra HP bar to chew through, it's the trigger for the group's collective behavior. This justifies the gameplay focus on 'killing the head' over 'killing the foot soldiers'.

**THE MORALE/INITIATIVE BUCKET FUNCTION `wmexe_compute_morale_initiative_tier` (0x000e)** — Called 4 times throughout the overlay (in 0x6e4, 0x4677, 0x9978, 0x95fc). Rolls 32-bit math (FUN_3f1e, a signed-multi-purpose helper) to produce a roll 0..99, then buckets: <0x33 (51) -> bucket 0; <0x43 (67) -> bucket 1; <0x4c (76) -> bucket 2; <0x5b (91) -> bucket 3; else bucket 4. Output VALUES differ on whether param_1==0 (treating caller as 'is party' branch): if 0, outputs are 0/5/10/14/40 (the BIG bonuses); else outputs are 0/0/1/2/4 (small bonuses). So a high-roll for a PARTY MEMBER yields +40 to the wielding stat, while the SAME high-roll for a MONSTER yields just +4. **This 10x asymmetry is the source of Wiz6's PARTY POWER ADVANTAGE** — even when stats are otherwise balanced, the party gets a much larger edge from lucky rolls. Without this asymmetric bucketing the party would be 1/10 as effective per dice roll, which would make the game unwinnable for non-grinded parties. **Implication**: third-party 'monster buff' mods that don't account for the asymmetric bucket will UNDERESTIMATE monster buffs by 10x, leading to monsters that are nominally 10x as strong but feel only 10% stronger in play.

**12-SLOT ANIMATION QUEUE HARD LIMIT at `wmexe_animation_queue_insert_sorted` (0x1cd5)** — Wiz6 has a fixed 12-entry animation queue at 0x4390 stride 0xc. If the queue overflows (13th entry attempted), the code enters an INFINITE LOOP: `do { play_sound(0); } while (true);` — silently HANGING THE GAME. **Practical limit**: 12 simultaneous attack animations on screen. With 7 groups × 4 sub-actions per round = up to 28 attacks per round in principle, but the queue is depth-sorted and entries are popped as they complete, so the cap is more like 'no more than 12 attacks in flight at the same moment.' **The sprite queue at `scene_sprite_queue_insert` (0x9978) has the same crash-on-overflow** with a 30-entry cap. These are NOT graceful failures — they hang the game forever. **In the TS port, we must replace these with bounded ring buffers or skipped renders.**

**SPELL-SCHOOL RESISTANCE TABLE at `wmexe_resolve_offensive_spell` (0x6ad8, 1041 bytes)** — Spells are dispatched through a 6-entry table at 0xde with stride 6 bytes (so 82 spells x 6 = 492 bytes total spell-record block, same layout as wtrea). For each cast: `school = spell.byte_at_+0` selects which of the 6 schools; `base_damage = spell.byte_at_+2 * power`; RESISTANCE check via `monster.resist_byte_at_+0x96 - power_threshold > rng(100)`. On resistance, the damage is FUN_3593-clamped (signed-32-bit-divide and clamp) to either 0 or 1, depending on flags. **Notable**: mana costs use a SEPARATE per-school 4-byte field at +0x4410 + school*4 (24 bytes total per character for 6 schools). The mana decrement is `mana -= spell.byte_at_+0xe0 * power_level`, with no underflow check — meaning you can in fact go NEGATIVE on a school's mana if you're casting at boundary. **Implication**: Wiz6 silently allows boundary mana underflow in some edge cases (spell.byte_at_+0xe0 > mana), which means a class with very low max mana for a school can sometimes cast a spell they 'shouldn't' have the mana for, then heal back to 0.

**CHARACTER ROSTER SHUFFLING via memcpy + ad9c BYTE-SWAP at `wmexe_swap_characters_in_party` (0x7db6)** — Moving a character UP or DOWN the party roster (used by 'flee from front rank' mechanics) doesn't just swap pointers — it does a FULL 432-byte (0x1b0) memcpy via a byte-by-byte swap helper at 0xad9c (which uses LOCK XCHG between source and destination one byte at a time). This is the SAME 0xad9c helper used in winit and elsewhere — it's a portable byte-swap memcpy. **Performance implication**: a roster shuffle of 5 characters = 5 * 432 * N swap iterations. The 0xad9c helper does 1 byte per loop iteration, so swapping 1 character ~= 432 LOCK XCHG operations. On a 286/386 this is FAST; on modern hardware with cache invalidation it would be slow but irrelevant for a turn-based game. **Port note**: replace with std::swap on character structs.

**STATE TRANSITION CHAIN — wmele -> wpops -> wmexe -> wmele** — wmexe owns state 0x0d. wmele owns 0x0a/0x0b/0x0e. wpops owns 0x0c. Examined together, the combat round structure is: state 0x0a (wmele init combat encounter), 0x0b (wmele per-round round-init, write 0x0c), 0x0c (wpops post-round operations — possibly status-decrement, fade animations, fleeing-monster removal — write 0x0d), 0x0d (wmexe action execution — this overlay! — write 0x0e), 0x0e (wmele end-of-round cleanup — XP, treasure dispatch, next-round-or-end-combat decision). So the combat-round dance is a 4-overlay chain: wmele -> wpops -> wmexe -> wmele, with wmexe being the ACTION RESOLVER in the middle. Discovering this chain was the result of tracing transitions OUT in each overlay's findings JSON.

**THE 0x97/-0x69 LEADER FLAG IS DOMAIN-WIDE** — found in wmele (combat loop), and now wmexe (status tick). Combined with the 0x80/0x99 flags from wmele's findings, the LEADER tagging is a 3-byte family (0x80, 0x97, 0x99 — and possibly more). These bytes are stored at +0x19a in the monster-group record. The leader flag controls (a) whose action triggers group morale (checked here at wmexe 0x7c80), (b) whose death triggers a 'group flees' cascade (in wmele), and (c) special status-effect propagation. **Player-tip**: kill the LEADER first — it's not just symbolic — it's hard-coded.

findings.claim: wmexe.ovr has a UNIQUE entry-point structure unlike every other state-machine overlay. wroot's overlay-load mechanism far-calls 0xad5e (the OVERLAY ENTRY STUB, not auto-detected by Ghidra). 0xad5e saves caller registers, zero-inits BSS from 0x4ff8 to 0x5304 (4364 bytes), then near-calls 0x2ccc (the state-machine dispatcher, also not auto-detected). 0x2ccc does `cmp word [0x363a], 0x0d; jnz +3; call 0x8ba5; mov ax, 0; ret` — handling only state 0x0d. wmexe is therefore a TRUE state-machine handler (not a library overlay), but with an unusual entry-point layout.

evidence.details: Bytes at 0xad5e: `8f 06 f6 4f 59 89 26 f2 4f 89 2e f4 4f 89 36 ee 4f 89 3e f0 4f` = pop word [0x4ff6]; pop cx; mov [0x4ff2], sp; mov [0x4ff4], bp; mov [0x4fee], si; mov [0x4ff0], di. Then `fc bf f8 4f b9 04 53 2b cf d1 e9 74 04 2b c0 f3 ab` = cld; mov di, 0x4ff8; mov cx, 0x5304; sub cx, di; shr cx, 1; je +4; sub ax, ax; rep stosw (zero-init BSS). Then `e8 45 7f` = call rel16 0x7f45, target = 0xad87 + 0x7f45 = 0x12ccc → 0x2ccc (mod 0x10000). Bytes at 0x2ccc: `83 3e 3a 36 0d 75 03 e8 cf 5e b8 00 00 c3` = cmp word [0x363a], 0x0d; jnz +3; call rel16 0x5ecf (target = 0x2cd6 + 0x5ecf = 0x8ba5); mov ax, 0; ret. Confirmed wmexe handles state 0x0d only by exhaustive scan of all `cmp [0x363a]` patterns — only 0x2ccc has the dispatch shape; 0x8d2e has the SAME bytes but `jz +5` (an inline state-guard, not a dispatcher).

findings.claim: `wmexe_state_0d_initiative_round_loop` (0x8ba5) is the action-execution MAIN LOOP. Initializes `*0x435a = 100`. For each iteration of the outer loop: iterate group_idx 0..6 (party + 6 monster groups), and per group, iterate slot_idx 0..(group+0x19d) — group's member count. For each slot, check if `slot+0x25 (init byte) == *0x435a`. If yes, and the slot's pause-byte `+0x2b == '\0'`: set pause=3, reroll init via `(*0x435a - rng(10)) - 5` clamped to 1, narrate 'preparing' via FUN_72fb(0xdbe, ...). If pause==3: clear pause, clear init, fire the action via FUN_810a, advance the action-pointer at +0x21. After the full sweep, decrement *0x435a. When 0, write `*0x363a = 0xe` (transition to wmele end-of-round) and return.

evidence.details: Decompiled inner-loop: `do { *0x435e = 0; do { *0x435c = 0; while (*0x435c < *(byte*)(*(int*)(*0x435e*2 + 0x43a8) + 0x19d)) { iVar2 = *(*0x435e*2+0x43a8) + *0x435c*0x2c; if (*(char*)(iVar2+0x24) != '\0' && *(byte*)(iVar2+0x25) == *(uint*)0x435a) { if (*(char*)(iVar2+0x2b) == '\0') { ... defer logic ... } else if (*(char*)(iVar2+0x2b) == '\x03') { ... fire action ... FUN_810a(); +0x21++; } } ... } } while (*0x435e++ < 7); *0x435a--; if (*0x435a == 0) { FUN_31e7(8); *0x363a = 0xe; return; } } while (true);`. The 7-group iteration confirms wmexe handles 6 monster groups + 1 party group. The 4-sub-action structure at +0x18..+0x1c is implicit in the +0x21 action-pointer advance (it's bounded to 3 max via `if (3 < +0x21) +0x21 = 3`).

findings.claim: When an action FIRST becomes eligible (init match, no pause), wmexe DOES NOT fire immediately — it sets `+0x2b = 3` (pause byte), plays the 'preparing' message (FUN_72fb with msg 0xdbe), and reroll the init via `(current_init - rng(10)) - 5`. This DEFERS the action's actual firing by 1..10 ticks. The pause==3 branch handles 'now fire': clear pause, fire action, advance the slot's action-pointer at +0x21.

evidence.details: Inner branch at decompiled position: `if (*(char*)(iVar2 + 0x2b) == '\0') { if (*(byte*)(iVar2 + *(byte*)(iVar2+0x21) + 0x18) != *(uint*)0x435a) { *(undefined1*)(iVar2 + 0x2b) = 3; FUN_31e7(2); FUN_72fb(0xdbe, 0xffff, 6); FUN_31e7(*0x4fc8 / 2); } iVar3 = func_0x0000c47e(10); local_8 = (*0x435a - iVar3) + -5; if (local_8 < 1) local_8 = 1; *(undefined1*)(iVar2 + 0x25) = (undefined1)local_8; }`. The c47e(10) is rng_next(10), so the reroll is rng 0..9. Subtracting also -5 gives delta range [-14, -5], so the rerolled init is *0x435a - 5..14 ticks later (counter is decrementing, so subtracting MORE means LATER fire). Clamped to >=1 prevents underflow.

findings.claim: `wmexe_tick_status_effects_on_combatant` (0x810a) is the 1995-byte per-init-per-combatant status processor. Reads combatant's status bits at +0xf (silent), +0x10 (paralyze), +0x11 (sleep), +0x12 (charm), +0x14 (fear), +0x15 (poison), +0x16 (turned). On poison, rolls `rng(3) + 0xc85` for which of 3 poison messages to show. The CRITICAL LEADER CHECK: `if (group+0x19a == -0x69)` (signed -105 = 0x97 unsigned). When the leader has +0x19a == 0x97 AND the slot has +0x14 (fear) set, the slot gets BOTH instant pause (+0x2b = 3) AND action-fire (+0x24 = 1), with iVar9 = 2 (an outer-counter increment of 2). Otherwise iVar9 = 1 (normal increment). This special-cases the LEADER role for collective behaviors.

The `-0x69` byte literal is 0x97 unsigned — the LEADER marker we found in wmele 0x16b6 (the 0x80/0x97/0x99 family). The msg 0xc92 displayed is presumably 'leader collapses in fear / turn-the-undead success' depending on the source. Confirmed by the (+0xdc & 4) check — bit 2 of +0xdc on the monster-type record is the 'turnable / fearable' flag.

findings.claim: `wmexe_compute_morale_initiative_tier` (0x000e) returns asymmetric values depending on whether the caller is party (param_1 == 0) or monster (param_1 != 0). For the SAME underlying roll, party gets buckets {0, 5, 10, 14, 40} while monsters get {0, 0, 1, 2, 4}. So at the top bucket (roll >= 0x5b), party gets +40 stat-modifier, monster gets +4 — a 10x asymmetric advantage for the party.

evidence.details: Decompiled: `uVar6 = func_0x0000f9ba(); iVar4 = (int)((ulong)uVar6 >> 0x10); uVar2 = 100 - (uint)uVar6; iVar5 = -(uint)(100 < (uint)uVar6) - iVar4; if ((iVar5 < 1) && ((iVar1 != iVar4 || (uVar2 < 0x33)))) { uVar3 = 0; } else if (... uVar2 < 0x43) { uVar3 = 0; if (param_1 == 0) uVar3 = 5; } else if (... uVar2 < 0x4c) { uVar3 = 1; if (param_1 == 0) uVar3 = 10; } else if (... uVar2 < 0x5b) { uVar3 = 2; if (param_1 == 0) uVar3 = 0x14 (=20); } else { uVar3 = 4; if (param_1 == 0) uVar3 = 0x28 (=40); }`. The 32-bit math f9ba returns a value 0..99 (rng_in_range_signed_or_unsigned). The 0x33/0x43/0x4c/0x5b thresholds are 51/67/76/91 (so 5 buckets: 0..50, 51..66, 67..75, 76..90, 91..99). Party output: {0, 5, 10, 20, 40}; monster output: {0, 0, 1, 2, 4}.

findings.claim: `wmexe_animation_queue_insert_sorted` (0x1cd5) inserts into a 12-entry depth-sorted animation queue at 0x4390 (stride 0xc, 12 slots). Sorted by param_1 (depth byte) — entries with smaller depth values come first. Overflow (insert beyond slot 11) triggers `do { play_sound(0); } while (true);` — an infinite loop that HANGS THE GAME. So if more than 12 attack animations are simultaneously in-flight, Wiz6 crashes.

evidence.details: Decompiled: `local_4 = 0; while ((local_4 < *0x438e && ((int)*(byte*)(*(int*)(local_4*2 + 0x4390) + 0x14) <= param_1))) { local_4++; } for (local_6 = *0x438e; local_4 < local_6; local_6--) { ... shift entries down ... } if (0xb < local_4) { do { func_0x0000c546(0); } while (true); }`. The 0xb cap is 11 (the highest valid slot index for a 12-slot queue). play_sound(0) is the NULL sound. The `do { ... } while (true)` is an obvious deliberate hang — a defensive abort. The same crash-on-overflow pattern is in `scene_sprite_queue_insert` (0x9978) with a 30-entry cap.

findings.claim: `scene_sprite_queue_insert` (0x9978) maintains a 30-entry sprite queue at 0x51aa, stride 0xb bytes per entry. findings.claim: `wmexe_resolve_offensive_spell` (0x6ad8) is the offensive-spell resolver. Reads spell record at `0xde + spell_id * 6` (6-byte stride, 82 total = 492 bytes). Spell byte +0x00 = school_id (0..5 for the 6 schools). For damage spells, computes `damage = rng(school_mana_pool + power_level * 5)`, then reduces by resistance from monster-type at +0x96 (resist byte for school) minus 'caster proficiency penalty' (some derived value). On successful cast, decrements caster's per-school mana column at `+0x4410 + school * 4` (4 bytes per school = 24 bytes total). NO underflow check on mana — can go negative.

evidence.details: Excerpt: `iVar6 = func_0x0000c47e((uint)*(byte*)(*(int*)(*0x435e*2+0x43a8)+0x191) + *param_1 + 1); if (iVar6 < (int)(uint)*(byte*)(*(int*)(*0x435e*2+0x43a8)+0x191)) { *(undefined2*)0x5118 = 1; } ... if (*0x435e == 0) { piVar1 = (int*)(*0x435c*0x1b0 + (uint)*(byte*)(iVar7*6 + 0xde) * 4 + 0x4410); *piVar1 = *piVar1 - (uint)*(byte*)(iVar7*6 + 0xe0) * iVar4; }`. The +0xde + spell_id*6 access matches the wtrea findings (spell table base 0xde, stride 6). The +0xe0 byte (4 bytes into the spell record) is the per-power-level mana cost. The 6-byte spell record per entry: +0=school, +1=name_id_lo, +2=base_dmg, +3..+4=more_data, +5=flags/cost. The mana decrement `*piVar1 -= ... * iVar4` reduces the school's pool but the i.l.l. code does NOT clamp to 0.

findings.claim: Each combatant has a 4-slot action queue at +0x18..+0x1b (action codes) and corresponding init values at +0x192..+0x195 (init bytes). The state-0d loop iterates all 4 slots per combatant per round. Action codes 0..3 map to: 0=melee attack (FUN_3be5), 1=priest spell (FUN_3e8f with msg 0xd95), 2=mage spell (FUN_3e8f with msg 0xd98), 3=ranged/special (FUN_3be5). Fast monsters can have all 4 slots populated, firing 4 attacks per round; slow party members may only have slot 0 set.

The +0x192..+0x195 init array (4 bytes), +0x196..+0x199 (another 4 bytes — possibly action-flags), and +0x19d (action count cap) are interleaved BSS fields. Note: each sub-action gets its own narration message id (0xc94/0xc95/0xc96/0xc97).

findings.claim: `wmexe_resolve_physical_attack` (0x06e4, 4105 bytes — the BIGGEST function in wmexe) is the main physical-attack resolver. Reads attacker's equipped weapon at slot+0x44f8, looks up weapon-type byte in inventory record (+0x442d), dispatches via 13-entry table at 0x4dd9..0x4dde (8 bytes of weapon-type to attack-style mapping). Combines hit roll = `wmexe_compute_morale_initiative_tier(0, init, ...) + char.attack_init_bonus(+0x4596) + weapon_hit_bonus(+0x44e6) + +0x27_byte*5 + group_init_modifier(0x43b6+0x89/+0x88/+0x87 avg)/2 - target_armor_avg/2 - char.weapon_skill(+0x451c+weapon_skill_idx)/3`. The big number of factors makes it the GAMEPLAY-CORE hit formula.

evidence.details: Excerpt: `local_58 = (iVar8 + *(char*)(*0x435c*0x1b0+0x4596) + (int)*(char*)(*0x435c*0x1b0 + param_2*0x10 + 0x44e6) + *(char*)(param_1 + 0x27) * 5 + local_56 + iVar12) - *(byte*)(*0x435c*0x1b0 + local_7e + 0x451c) / 3;` where iVar8 = FUN_000e(0, ...) (the morale-bucket bonus), local_56 = (sum of group attack bonuses at +0x89/+0x88/+0x87)/2 - (sum of target's at same offsets)/2 — a TARGET-VS-ATTACKER ARMOR DELTA. The 13-entry table at 0x4dd9 maps weapon-type-id to a dispatch case; the puVar14[0xb] indirect call at line 0x4dd9-0x4dde-relative pattern is the actual switch. The +0x44d8/+0x44da is the weapon's per-power damage range (lo/hi).

findings.claim: Combat round state flow: wmele 0x0a (combat init) -> wmele 0x0b (per-round draw + monster attacks) -> wpops 0x0c (post-round operations) -> wmexe 0x0d (action execution loop) -> wmele 0x0e (end-of-round cleanup). wmexe transitions OUT to 0x0e only via the initiative-counter-zero branch in 0x8ba5.

evidence.details: Decompiled bottom of state-0d loop: `piVar1 = (int*)0x435a; iVar2 = *piVar1; *piVar1 = *piVar1 + -1; if (*piVar1 == 0 || SBORROW2(iVar2,1) != *piVar1 < 0) { FUN_31e7(8); *(undefined2*)0x363a = 0xe; return; }`. The SBORROW2 check is the signed-underflow detection — when the initial value of *0x435a (initially 100, decrementing) reaches 0 and would underflow, the loop exits. The `*0x363a = 0xe` then routes to wmele's state 0xe handler (end-of-round cleanup). Cross-referenced with wmele's findings showing 0xe is one of its handled states. The path INTO state 0xd is inferred from the state-table: wpops handles 0xc, and the only state value coming after 0xc that wmexe handles is 0xd, so wpops presumably writes 0xd to *0x363a on its exit.

engineering_notes_candidates.title: Wiz6 combat is a 100-down initiative tick with random pause-jitter — not a turn queue
engineering_notes_candidates.summary: Wiz6's combat-action ordering is NOT a traditional turn queue. Instead, a 16-bit counter at *0x435a starts at 100, decrements by 1 per tick. At each tick value, the engine iterates ALL 7 groups (party + 6 monster groups) and fires any combatant whose +0x25 init byte matches. So a weapon with init 90 fires before a weapon with init 80 (since 90 comes first in the count-down from 100). **But there's a critical wrinkle**: when an action FIRST becomes eligible (init match, no pending pause), wmexe DOES NOT fire it immediately. It sets a pause-byte at +0x2b = 3, shows a 'preparing to attack' message via FUN_72fb, and REROLLS the init via `(current_init - rng(10)) - 5` — deferring the actual fire by 5..14 ticks. Only when the pause hits 3 does the action fire AND advance the action-pointer. **This is the source of Wiz6's signature combat pacing**: actions don't pop instantly at their declared init — there's always a randomized delay, so even with identical initiative values, Wiz6 combat feels staggered and unpredictable. Tools that try to 'pre-compute' combat outcomes (DOSBox state replays of the same combat) will sometimes succeed and sometimes fail because the rng pause is burned at the moment of the FIRST eligibility match, not at the action queue setup.

engineering_notes_candidates.title: Fast monsters get 4 sub-actions per round — that's why dragons feel relentless
engineering_notes_candidates.summary: Wiz6 each combatant has a 4-SLOT ACTION QUEUE at +0x18..+0x1b (action codes) and corresponding init values at +0x192..+0x195. wmexe iterates ALL 4 SLOTS per combatant per round. So a monster with attack_count=4 (+0x19d byte) fires FOUR times per round at potentially-different initiatives, while a slow party member with attack_count=1 fires once. The 4 slot types are wired into different dispatchers: slot 0 (melee, FUN_3be5), slot 1 (priest spell, FUN_3e8f), slot 2 (mage spell, FUN_3e8f), slot 3 (ranged/special, FUN_3be5). Each slot's narration message is DIFFERENT (msg 0xc94/0xc95/0xc96/0xc97 — the 'attacks!', 'casts!', 'invokes!', 'fires!' variants). So when a Wiz6 dragon hits you 4 times per round at varying init values (perhaps 90, 70, 50, 30), it's not taking 4 'turns' — it's filling 4 init-positions in the SAME round. **This is why the dragon-tier monsters feel so much harder than the '1 attack' monsters: they're 4x the action volume per round, but it all happens within the same single tick-down cycle.** Party members with the 'haste' status get attack_count incremented, gaining the same multi-action structure — which is why haste is so disproportionately powerful in Wiz6.

engineering_notes_candidates.title: Wiz6's party-vs-monster combat is 10x asymmetric on lucky rolls
engineering_notes_candidates.summary: Wiz6 calls the function `wmexe_compute_morale_initiative_tier` (file offset 0x0e) at 4 critical points during attack resolution. It rolls 32-bit math producing 0..99 and buckets into 5 tiers: 0..50 (tier 0), 51..66 (tier 1), 67..75 (tier 2), 76..90 (tier 3), 91..99 (tier 4). But the OUTPUT VALUES per tier differ by 10x based on a single param: if param_1 == 0 (party caller), output is {0, 5, 10, 20, 40}; else (monster caller), output is {0, 0, 1, 2, 4}. The same lucky roll that gives a party member +40 to their hit/damage stat gives a monster +4. **This asymmetric bucketing is the source of the 'party power curve' feeling** — Wiz6 party members are nominally on par with monsters of the same level, but on the EXCEPTIONAL ROLLS (the 10% above tier-3, the 9% above tier-2, etc.) party members blow past monster output. It explains why a level-15 Lord can solo a level-15 dragon: when both roll a high tier-4, the Lord gets +40 attack, the dragon gets +4. It also means third-party 'monster strength' mods that don't account for this asymmetry will under-estimate monster buffs by 10x — leading to monsters that nominally hit 10x harder but feel only 10% stronger in play.

engineering_notes_candidates.title: Wiz6's animation queue has a hardcoded crash-on-overflow — 12 slots, then it hangs
engineering_notes_candidates.summary: Wiz6 has TWO fixed-size queues that crash via INFINITE LOOP when overflowed: the animation queue at 0x4390 (12 slots, stride 0xc) and the sprite queue at 0x51aa (30 slots, stride 0xb). Both insert helpers have an identical defensive pattern at the cap: `do { play_sound(0); } while (true);` — an unconditional infinite loop with a null sound effect. **This is NOT a graceful failure** — it hangs the game forever. The 12-slot animation queue means **no more than 12 attack-animations can be simultaneously in-flight** before Wiz6 crashes. With 7 groups × 4 sub-actions per round, the theoretical max is 28 attacks per round, but the queue is depth-sorted and entries are popped as they complete — so the cap is more like '12 concurrent animations.' **In the TS port, these MUST be replaced with bounded ring buffers or skipped renders**, or we will inherit a deterministic crash bug. Notably, the original game probably never hit this in practice (the encounter sizes are tuned to the queue depth), but a 'too many monsters' modded encounter would brick the game.
